title: A gentle food waste diary
description: Writing down what gets thrown away for one week, without blame, shows exactly where a household can waste less.

body.heading: Notice before you change
paragraphs: For one ordinary week, keep a notebook or phone note near the bin and jot down any food that gets thrown away: what it was, roughly how much, and why. Forgotten leftovers, bread that went stale, salad that wilted: all of it counts, and none of it needs a lecture attached.
The diary works because memory is unreliable. Most people are surprised less by the total than by the pattern: it is usually the same two or three items, bought hopefully and eaten rarely.

body.heading: Read the pattern kindly
paragraphs: At the end of the week, look for repeats. If milk is always half-wasted, a smaller bottle or a different buying day solves it. If vegetables for a recipe always linger, frozen versions may serve the same meals with none of the race against the clock.
Share the findings as information, not accusation. In most households everyone contributes a little, and the fixes are about shopping and storage habits rather than anyone's character.

body.heading: Turn one finding into one change
paragraphs: Pick the single biggest repeat item and change just that: buy less of it, store it where you will see it, or plan a specific meal that uses it. One change kept is worth more than a grand overhaul abandoned by Thursday.
Repeat the diary for a week every few months. Seasons change what we eat, and the diary quietly keeps the household honest about whether the improvement stuck.

takeaway: Track what is thrown away for a week, find the repeat item, and change that one thing first.
